'''Lanhydrock House''', commonly known simply as '''Lanhydrock''',  is a country house and estate in the parish of [[Lanhydrock]], [[Cornwall]], England.

The house stands in extensive grounds of {{convert|890|acre}} above the [[River Fowey]], and has been owned and managed by the [[National Trust]] since 1953. The house dates from the 1620s, however most of the interiors were reconstructed after a fire in 1881; a new service wing was built at the same time. It is a Grade I [[listed building]] and is set in gardens with formal areas. The hill behind the house is planted with a fine selection of shrubs and trees.

The [[St Hydroc's Church, Lanhydrock|parish church]] is dedicated to St Hydroc and stands in the grounds of Lanhydrock House. Parts date back to the late 15th century and the church has a chancel, nave, north and south aisles and three-stage battlemented tower with nine bells. Eight bells date from the late 19th century and are regularly rung. The ninth bell dates from circa 1599 and is only rung infrequently for [[Funeral toll|tolling]].

==Early history==
[[File:Lanhydrock corridor.jpg|thumb|A corridor within the property]]
Lanhydrock estate belonged to the [[Augustinians|Augustinian]] priory of [[St Petroc]] at Bodmin but the [[Dissolution of the Monasteries]] during the 1530s saw it pass into private hands. In 1620 wealthy merchant Sir Richard Robartes, of [[Truro]], acquired the estate and began building Lanhydrock House, designed to a four-sided layout around a central courtyard and constructed of grey [[granite]]. Robartes died in 1624 but work on the building was continued by his son [[John Robartes, 1st Earl of Radnor]], a notable public figure who served as [[Lord Privy Seal]] and [[Lord President of the Council]]. The embattled walls were built of rude (rough), massive granite blocks with years 1636 and 1642 on the walls, indicating when they were built. A [[barbican]] gate was added and the house was garrisoned by [[English Civil War|Parliamentary forces]] in August 1644 when [[Sir Richard Grenville, 1st Baronet]] took possession.<ref name="cman143">{{cite news|title=Great Fire at Lanhydrock House, The Seat of Lord Robartes|work=The Cornishman|issue=143|date=7 April 1881|page=5}}</ref>

==Agar-Robartes==
Most of the current building dates from late Victorian times, when the estate came under the ownership of the Agar-Robartes family.

[[Henry Robartes, 3rd Earl of Radnor]] (c. 1695–1741), was succeeded as [[Earl of Radnor]] by a cousin, but decided to separate the estate from the peerages by leaving it to a son of his sister Mary. By the late 18th century it had passed to Anna Maria Hunt (1771–1861) of Mayfair, London, the great-niece of the third Earl. In 1804 she married Charles Bagenal Agar, the youngest son of Irish peer [[James Agar, 1st Viscount Clifden]]. The couple had three children, but by 1818 not only had her husband died, but also her eldest and youngest sons. Resultantly, over the next fifty years of widowhood, although mainly an absentee landlord – she preferred the social life of London – she was known to be a conscientious, benevolent, and charitable landlord and employer, who greatly improved the estate. On the death of his mother in 1822, her surviving middle son [[Thomas Agar-Robartes, 1st Baron Robartes|Thomas Agar]] took up residence at Lanhydrock and adopted the Robartes name by royal warrant. Agar-Robartes was returned to Parliament for [[East Cornwall (UK Parliament constituency)|Cornwall East]] in 1847, a seat he held until 1868. In 1869 the barony of Robartes held by his mother's ancestors was revived when he was raised to the peerage as Baron Robartes of Lanhydrock and of [[Truro]] in the County of Cornwall. By 1872 Lord Robartes of Lanhydrock was listed among the top ten landowners in Cornwall, with estates of {{convert|22234|acre|ha}} or 2.93% of Cornwall.{{cn|date=June 2025}}

[[File:Lanhydrock Galerie 2010.jpg|thumb|The Long Gallery]]
Agar-Robartes had the east wing of the house demolished, leaving the U-shaped plan seen today. In 1880 he commissioned the architect [[George Gilbert Scott]] to renovate Lanhydrock House. On 4 April 1881 a major fire destroyed the south wing and caused extensive damage to the central section. The fire started in the kitchen, and a near gale-force wind fanned the flames along the south wing and the ″communicating block″.<ref name="cman143"/> Of the main house only the north wing, with its {{convert|116|feet}} Long Gallery, and the front porch building survived intact, along with the original gatehouse, which dates from the mid-17th century. The gallery was decorated with old plaster work which was considered to be the finest of its type in the west of England with figures representing the creation in ″bas-relief″. The property was insured for £10,000 in the Royal Standard Office and for £10,000 in the County Fire Office, and the damage is estimated to have cost £8,000 to £10,000<ref name="cman143"/> It was reported in August 1881 that the rebuilding of the house would cost £50,000 and was to be undertaken by Messers Lang and Son of [[Liskeard]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Local News|work=The Cornishman|issue=162|date=18 August 1881|page=6}}</ref> New sections were built behind the south wing, including a kitchen block, in the style of the original building – which was unusual at the time. Agar-Robartes’s wife died five days after the fire of smoke inhalation, and he died twelve months later, reported to be of a broken heart.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/lanhydrock/features/salvation-and-tragedy-1798-1881|title=Salvation and tragedy: 1798–1881|publisher= National Trust|access-date= 24 January 2018}}</ref>

Their only son, [[Thomas Charles Agar-Robartes, 6th Viscount Clifden|Thomas Charles Agar-Robartes]], inherited the estate. Having been [[called to the Bar]] in 1870, in 1880 Agar-Robartes was returned to Parliament as one of two representatives for Cornwall East. He appointed a local architect, [[Richard Coad]] – who had worked as an assistant to George Gilbert Scott – to design and supervise the construction of a high-Victorian house from the previous adaptions of the [[Jacobethan|Jacobean]] house his father had planned. After renovations on the house  were completed, Agar-Robartes moved his family there about 1885. Agar-Robartes entered the [[House of Lords]] on the death of his father in 1882,<ref>{{Rayment-hc|c|6|date=October 2012}}</ref> and on 10 September 1899 succeeded his kinsman as [[Viscount Clifden]]. In 1891, as chairman of the Agar-Robartes Bank, he took over the ownership of [[Wimpole Hall]], the largest house in Cambridgeshire. Moving his family home there, he later served as [[Lord-Lieutenant of Cambridgeshire]] from 1906 to 1915.

[[File:Lanhydrock House Billardzimmer 2014.jpg|thumb|Lanhydrock House – Billiard Room 2014]]
The Robartes family suffered great losses  during the [[First World War]], including the heir [[Thomas Agar-Robartes]], who was killed during the [[Battle of Loos]] in [[France]], while trying to rescue a colleague from no-man's land.<ref>{{Cite newspaper The Times |title=House of Commons War Memorial: Final Volumes Unveiled by The Speaker|date=6 February 1932 |page=7|issue=46050}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|editor-last=Moss-Blundell|editor-first=Edward Whitaker|title=The House of Commons Book of Remembrance 1914–1918|publisher=E. Mathews & Marrot|year=1931}}</ref> As Agar-Robartes was unmarried, his younger brother [[Francis Agar-Robartes, 7th Viscount Clifden|Francis]] later succeeded their father.

In 1951 the house was designated a Grade I [[listed building]].<ref>{{NHLE |num=1157870 |access-date=22 April 2007}}</ref>

==Antiquities==
[[File:Lanhydrock House.jpg|thumb|Lanhydrock Church]]
The [[St Hydroc's Church, Lanhydrock|parish church]] is dedicated to St Hydroc and stands in the grounds of Lanhydrock House. Parts date back to the late 15th century and the church has a chancel, nave, north and south aisles and three-stage battlemented tower with nine bells. Eight bells date from the late 19th century and are regularly rung. The ninth bell dates from circa 1599 and is only rung infrequently for [[Funeral toll|tolling]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://dove.cccbr.org.uk/detail.php?DoveID=LANHYDROCK|title=Dove Details|website=dove.cccbr.org.uk|access-date=11 July 2016}}</ref>

Arthur Langdon (1896) recorded two Cornish crosses and two cross bases (at Tredinnick Cross and Reperry)<ref>For more details of Reperry Cross, see [[Lanivet]]</ref> in the parish. One cross is in the churchyard and the other is half a cross head at Treffry. The cross in the churchyard is ornamented on all four sides of the shaft.<ref>Langdon, A. G. (1896) ''Old Cornish Crosses''. Truro: Joseph Pollard; pp. 382–83, 183, 227 & 423</ref> In addition to these there is a cross called Bodwen Cross; this cross was recorded in 1850 but was not mentioned by J. T. Blight or Arthur Langdon. It was found again in 1937 near [[Helman Tor]] in the parish of Lanlivery. It was taken from there and erected in the new cemetery at Lanhydrock. A request for it to be returned to Lanlivery to a site on the Saints' Way was refused.<ref>Langdon, A. G. (2002) ''Stone Crosses in Mid Cornwall''; 2nd ed. Federation of Old Cornwall Societies; p. 42</ref>

==Lanhydrock Estate Company==
In 1934, to manage income taxes and death duties, the entire Cornish landholdings of the Agar-Robartes family were incorporated into the Lanhydrock Estate Company. In 1953, faced with crippling death duties through a lack of his own children, the 7th Viscount Clifden gave the house and approximately {{convert|160|ha|acre|abbr=off}} of parkland to the [[National Trust]].<ref>[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-vh/w-visits/w-findaplace/w-lanhydrock.htm National Trust website: Lanhydrock] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100430133718/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-vh/w-visits/w-findaplace/w-lanhydrock.htm |date=30 April 2010 }}; retrieved May 2010</ref> This allowed the preservation of the house and its extensive Victorian collections, and, by agreement with the [[Inland Revenue]], payment in kind of death duties, allowing the residual Lanhydrock Estate Company to pass into the hands of the wider family.

On the death of the 7th Viscount, the titles and control of the company passed to his youngest brother [[Arthur Agar-Robartes, 8th Viscount Clifden]]. Lord Clifden died in December 1974, and in a similar death duty exchange with HM Revenue, added {{convert|298|acre}} during the 1970s to the National Trust's estate holdings.<ref>{{cite web|title=Lanhydrock in the 20th century|publisher=National Trust|access-date=14 January 2020|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/lanhydrock/features/lanhydrock-in-the-20th-century}}</ref> He had married Patience Mary Basset in 1920 but died without male issue, and upon his death all his titles, with the exception of the [[Viscount Clifden#Barons Mendip .281794.29|barony of Mendip]] (which the [[Shaun Agar, 6th Earl of Normanton|6th Earl of Normanton]] succeeded) became extinct. His daughter Rachel married Captain Cromwell Lloyd-Davies in 1941, and they had a daughter Ann Lloyd-Davies (1942–present). In 1964 she married Colin Williams; they and their three children now control the company.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://family-tree.cobboldfht.com/tree/view/person:4804|title = Family Tree – the Cobbold Family History Trust}}</ref>

As of 2020 the company owns and controls {{convert|2500|acre}} of land, and is by descent controlled by the Williams family.

==House and gardens today==
Today, the public tour of Lanhydrock house is one of the longest of any National Trust house. It takes in the service rooms, nurseries and some servants' bedrooms, as well as the main reception rooms and family bedrooms. In 2004 it was one of the Trust's ten most visited paid-entry properties, with over 200,000 visitors.{{cn|date=June 2025}}

Parts of the estate have been designated as an [[Important Plant Area]], by the organisation [[Plantlife]], for its [[ancient woodland]] and [[lichen]]s.<ref>{{cite web|title=Lanhydrock Park|url=http://www.plantlife.org.uk/wild_plants/important_plant_areas/lanhydrock_park|publisher=[[Plantlife]]|access-date=7 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120701021511/http://www.plantlife.org.uk/wild_plants/important_plant_areas/lanhydrock_park/|archive-date=1 July 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref> The hill behind the house is planted with a fine selection of shrubs and trees.<ref>{{cite web|title=Lanhydrock|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/lanhydrock/things-to-see-and-do/article-1355827937917/|publisher=National Trust}}</ref>

Lanhydrock was the main setting for the [[Twelfth Night (1996 film)| 1996 film version of ''Twelfth Night'']] directed by [[Trevor Nunn]], and starring [[Helena Bonham Carter]] as Olivia.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cornwall-calling.co.uk/film-television/twelfth-night.htm|title=Twelfth Night|website=www.cornwall-calling.co.uk}}</ref> On 12 June 2008 Lanhydrock hosted an episode of BBC TV's  ''[[Antiques Roadshow]]'', which was first aired on 12 October 2008 (part 1) and 30 November 2008 (part 2).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b00f2dfs|title=BBC One - Antiques Roadshow, Series 31, Lanhydrock|website=BBC}}</ref>

From 2024 the [[Jacobean architecture|Jacobean]] plasterwork ceiling in the Long Gallery, one of the few parts of the house that survived the 1881 fire, was the subject of a conservation project to clean and restore it.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/cornwall/lanhydrock/lanhydrock-ceiling-convservation-project |title=Lanhydrock Long Gallery ceiling conservation project |website=nationaltrust.org.uk |access-date=22 June 2025}}</ref> In June 2025 the restoration featured in an episode of BBC's series ''Hidden Treasures of the National Trust''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/iplayer/episode/m002cg6w/hidden-treasures-of-the-national-trust-series-3-6-raising-the-roof|title=Hidden Treasures of the National Trust – Series 3: 6. Raising the Roof!|via=www.bbc.co.uk}}</ref>

1100874.title: Godrevy
1100874.extract: Godrevy (Cornish: Godrevi, meaning small farms) ( gə-DREE-vee) is an area on the eastern side of St Ives Bay, west Cornwall, England, United Kingdom, which faces the Atlantic Ocean. It is popular with both the surfing community and walkers. It is part owned by the National Trust, and offshore on Godrevy Island is a lighthouse maintained by Trinity House which is said to be the inspiration for Virginia Woolf's novel To the Lighthouse. Godrevy lies within the Cornwall Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (AONB) and the South West Coast Path runs around the whole promontory. There are several public car parks on the western side where the National Trust owns and operates a café.

It is popular with both the [[surfing]] community and walkers. It is part owned by the [[National Trust]], and offshore on Godrevy Island is a [[Godrevy Lighthouse|lighthouse]] maintained by [[Trinity House]] which is said to be the inspiration for [[Virginia Woolf|Virginia Woolf's]] novel ''[[To the Lighthouse]]''.<ref name=thomas>{{cite book|last=Thomas|first=Charles|title=Godrevy Light|year=2009|publisher=Twelveheads Press|isbn=9780906294703|author2=Mann, Jessica}}</ref> Godrevy lies within the [[Cornwall Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty]] (AONB) and the [[South West Coast Path]] runs around the whole promontory. There are several public car parks on the western side where the National Trust owns and operates a café.<ref name=Godrevy>{{cite web|title=Godrevy|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/godrevy/|publisher=National Trust|access-date=15 November 2012}}</ref>

== Godrevy Head ==
[[File:Godrevy Cornwall map.png|thumb|Map of Godrevy Head]]
The headland ({{gbmapping|SW580430}}) is on the [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic]] coast in [[Cornwall]] on the eastern side of [[St Ives, Cornwall|St Ives]] Bay and about three miles (5 km) northeast of the town of [[Hayle]]. The nearest village is [[Gwithian]], half a mile west beyond Godrevy Bridge across the [[Red River, Cornwall|Red River]]. The [[promontory]] is roughly square in shape and faces north into the Atlantic occupying an area of approximately {{convert|1|sqmi|km2|adj=on}}. In 1939, {{convert|320|acre|ha}} and {{convert|5|mi|km}} of coastline was donated to the National Trust by D. W. Thomas of Gwithian, followed by a further {{convert|19|acre|ha}} of land adjoining Godrevy Farm in 1962 by Nicholas and [[Charles Thomas (historian)|Charles Thomas]].<ref name=thomas/> Godrevy Head has some of the best coastal [[heathland]] in Cornwall, with many species of plant, animal and insect life. Part of the headland, along with the coast to the east, was designated as part of the [[Godrevy Head to St Agnes]] SSSI ([[Site of Special Scientific Interest]]) in 1951.<ref>{{cite web|title=Godrevy Head to St Agnes|url=http://www.sssi.naturalengland.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1003195.pdf|publisher=[[Natural England]]|access-date=6 December 2011|year=1989|archive-date=24 October 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121024212616/http://www.sssi.naturalengland.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1003195.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The western side of Godrevy Head is bounded by rocks to the north and a wide sandy beach to the south which is popular for [[surfing]]. At the north-western corner of the headland is Godrevy Point; at the north-eastern corner is Navax Point ({{langx|kw|Penn Kynyavos}}, meaning ''head of the autumn dwelling''){{cn|date=October 2015}}. The cliffs between the two points are approximately {{convert|220|ft}} above sea level.

On the northern side of the headland are two coves named Mutton Cove and Kynance Cove ({{langx|kw|Porth Kynyavos}}, meaning ''cove of the autumn dwelling'') beyond which the Nathaga Rocks ({{langx|kw|Lethegow}}, meaning ''milky ones'') lie off Navax Point. On the eastern side of the headland are Castle Giver Cove ({{langx|kw|Porth Castel Gaver}}, meaning ''cove of the goat's castle'') and Fishing Cove.

South of Navax Point is an area of heath named The Knavocks ({{langx|kw|Kynyavos}}, meaning ''autumn dwelling'') which is managed by The National Trust. The grassland and gorse scrub is criss-crossed with footpaths and is home to many species of butterflies and birds, notably nesting [[European stonechat]]s. The Knavocks, like other coastal heathlands in Cornwall, is managed by regularly cutting back the gorse and by grazing, the National Trust having introduced a herd of ponies for the purpose.

Beyond Fishing Cove, the coast swings to the east towards [[Hell's Mouth, Cornwall|Hell's Mouth]] and North Cliffs. The land here rises to approximately {{convert|290|ft}}, the highest point on this section of clifftop.

The cliffs, offshore rocks and coast around Godrevy Head form a renowned habitat for seabirds including cormorants, fulmars, guillemots, and razorbills and several species of gull. There is also a substantial population of grey seals throughout the year. Occasionally, bottlenose dolphins can be seen in the area.

==Godrevy Island and The Stones==
[[File:Godrevy Island 2 (2382442503).jpg|thumb|right|Godrevy Island.]]
Godrevy Island lies approx three hundred yards off Godrevy Point. The uninhabited island is the site of [[Godrevy Lighthouse]], operated by [[Trinity House]]. The island covers an area of {{convert|12|acres}} and is home to seagulls, oystercatchers and pipits. Its vegetation is dominated by grasses, with primroses and [[sea thrift]] flowering in the spring. Landings may only be made on the island with the permission of Trinity House.<ref name="BoothPerrott1981">{{cite book|last1=Booth|first1=David|last2=Perrott|first2=David|title=The Shell Book of the Islands of Britain|year=1981|publisher=Guideway/Windward|isbn=0711200874|page=152}}</ref>

Seaward of Godrevy Island is a submerged reef known as The Stones, which extends for approximately {{convert|1|mi}} to the northwest across the eastern approach to St Ives Bay. It has been the site of many sinkings over the years but it was not until the disastrous loss of the [[SS Nile (1850)|SS ''Nile'']] on 30 November 1854, with the loss of all aboard, that Trinity House was pressured to construct a lighthouse on the island. It was built in 1859 and was converted to fully automatic operation in 1939.<ref name="BoothPerrott1981" />

== Geology ==
The rocks at Godrevy are [[Devonian]] [[mudstones]] overlain with [[Quaternary]] [[ice age|ice age deposits]]. The mudstone was laid in a deep sea sedimentary basin and subject to [[seismic]] activity, forming [[turbidites]]. Under gravitational slumping the coarser material settled first followed by the finer material.<ref name=CSM>{{cite web|title=Godrevy coastal exposures|url=http://projects.exeter.ac.uk/geomincentre/excur-godrevy.htm|work=CSM Virtual Museum|publisher=Camborne School of Mines|access-date=16 December 2012}}</ref>

Overlying the turbidites are a sequence of rocks laid down during recent ice ages, and Godrevy is considered to be one of the most important [[Pleistocene]] (2,588,000 to 11,700 years ago) sites in the south-west of England. Mammal [[fossils]] are rare in Cornwall and a dog was found within the poorly sorted, coarse-grained sediments of [[head]] dated between 12,000 and 15,000 years ago. The earliest evidence of canine domestication is a dog, or possible a wolf puppy, in a human burial site in [[Israel]] from 12,000 years ago. The earliest British domestic dog remains are from [[Starr Carr]], [[Yorkshire]], dated to 9,538 (± 350) BP. In order to date the skeleton and to test [[hypotheses|three hypotheses]], part of a bone was sampled at the [[Oxford University]] Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit using [[accelerator mass spectrometry]] (AMS).<ref name=Crisp>{{cite journal|last=Crisp|first=G|author2=Pirrie D |author3=Shail R K |author4=Sabin R C |title=The Godrevy dog; early canine or lost pet?|journal=Geoscience in South-west England|year=2001|volume=10|issue=2|url=http://www.ussher.org.uk/journal/00s/2001/documents/Crisp_et_al_2001.pdf|access-date=16 December 2012|publisher=Usher Society}}</ref>

The three hypotheses were:
* if the skeleton is in context with the geology (i.e. the same age as the head deposits), then the deposits are younger than previously thought,
* if the dating of the head deposits is correct, then the dog is a very early example of domestication,
* if the skeleton is younger, it is not in context with the geology.

The dog skeleton dates to 1650 AD (± 30), which implies that it is possible for a recently dead animal to be within ice age deposits but leave no indication of how it happened. Fossil occurrence within ice age deposits need to be treated with caution, and skeletal remains need to be dated by AMS to provide their actual age and geological significance.<ref name=Crisp/>

==Religion==
The Godrevy team ministry within the Church of England Diocese of Truro includes five churches in the St Ives district.<ref>[http://www.achurchnearyou.com/phillack-st-felicitas/ Phillack Parish Church of St Felicitas and St Piala]</ref>

3449994.title: Hawker's Hut
3449994.extract:
Hawker's Hut is an historic hut at Morwenstow, Cornwall originally built by the eccentric clergyman, poet and antiquarian, Robert Stephen Hawker (1803 – 1875), close to Higher Sharpnose Point. The hut is located approximately 1 mile from Morwenstow Church.
The hut is mainly of timber construction and is partially built into the hillside (earth sheltered) with a turf roof.  It was originally built from driftwood and timber retrieved from shipwrecks by the eccentric vicar and poet. Parson Hawker spent many hours in the hut writing poems and smoking opium, perhaps inspired by the views of the Atlantic Ocean. Visitors to the hut during Hawker's time there included Alfred Tennyson in 1848 (with whom Hawker toured Tintagel) and Charles Kingsley. Today the hut is accessible on foot from the coastal footpath via a short set of steps.
Hawker's hut has been maintained since its original construction although some of the original elements are still present. It is currently the smallest property belonging to the National Trust.

'''Hawker's Hut''' is an historic hut at [[Morwenstow]], [[Cornwall]] originally built by the eccentric clergyman, poet and [[antiquarian]], [[Robert Stephen Hawker]] (1803 – 1875), close to Higher Sharpnose Point. The hut is located approximately 1 mile from [[Church of St Morwenna and St John the Baptist, Morwenstow|Morwenstow Church]].

The hut is mainly of timber construction and is partially built into the hillside (earth sheltered) with a turf roof.  It was originally built from driftwood and timber retrieved from shipwrecks by the eccentric vicar and poet. Parson Hawker spent many hours in the hut writing poems and smoking [[opium]], perhaps inspired by the views of the [[Atlantic]] Ocean.<ref>Clegg, David (2005) ''Cornwall & the Isles of Scilly: the complete guide''. Leicester: Matador; pp. 46-47</ref> Visitors to the hut during Hawker's time there included [[Alfred Tennyson, 1st Baron Tennyson|Alfred Tennyson]] in 1848<ref>Hale, A., "The Land Near the Dark Cornish Sea" in: ''Journal for the Academic Study of Magic'', Issue 2, pp. 206-225</ref> (with whom Hawker toured Tintagel) and [[Charles Kingsley]]. Today the hut is accessible on foot from the coastal footpath via a short set of steps.

Hawker's hut has been maintained since its original construction although some of the original elements are still present. It is currently the smallest property belonging to the [[National Trust]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.atlasobscura.com/places/hawkers-hut |title=Hawker's Hut |website=Atlas Obscura |language=en |access-date=2019-08-30}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://rshawker.co.uk/history/ |title=History | website=rshawker.co.uk |access-date=2019-08-30}}</ref>

It is situated on the Lizard peninsula approximately two miles (3 km) north of Lizard Point. The cove became popular in the early Victorian era, with many distinguished visitors including Queen Victoria and Prince Albert and the poets Alfred Tennyson and Algernon Swinburne. The BBC has described Kynance Cove as "one of the most beautiful stretches of coastline in the South West". The South West Coast Path, which follows the coast of south west England from Somerset to Dorset passes by on the cliffs overlooking the cove.
Kynance Cove and the surrounding coast are owned and managed by the National Trust. It is part of the West Lizard Site of Special Scientific Interest and is in the Cornwall Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. The Kynance Café, which opened for business in 1929, relied on spring water and on a generator for power. When the café became the property of the National Trust in 1999, the Trust renovated it and provided mains water and electricity. Access is via the coastal footpath from the nearby National Trust car park.

'''Kynance Cove''' ({{langx|kw|Ben Kewnans}}, meaning ''foot of steep-sided valley'') is a [[cove]] on the eastern side of [[Mount's Bay]], [[Cornwall]], England. It is situated on the [[The Lizard|Lizard peninsula]] approximately two miles (3 km) north of [[Lizard Point, Cornwall|Lizard Point]].<ref name=os>Ordnance Survey, Explorer Map 103, The Lizard, Falmouth and Helston. {{ISBN|978-0-319-23704-5}}</ref> The cove became popular in the early [[Victorian era]], with many distinguished visitors including [[Queen Victoria]] and [[Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha|Prince Albert]]<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=GmbGCQAAQBAJ&pg=PT158 Penzance: The Biography, Mike Sagar-Fenton, page 158]</ref> and the poets [[Alfred Tennyson, 1st Baron Tennyson|Alfred Tennyson]] and [[Algernon Swinburne]].<ref>[http://www.objectiveone.com/client/media/media-343.htm Kynance visits by Alfred Tennyson], objectiveone.com. Accessed 28 July 2023.</ref> The [[BBC]] has described Kynance Cove as "one of the most beautiful stretches of coastline in the South West".<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20070313094630/http://www.bbc.co.uk/england/sevenwonders/southwest/south-west-cornwall/index.shtml South-West Cornwall], bbc.co.uk. Accessed 28 July 2023.</ref> The [[South West Coast Path]], which follows the coast of south west England from [[Somerset]] to [[Dorset]] passes by on the cliffs overlooking the cove.<ref name=os/>

Kynance Cove and the surrounding coast are owned and managed by the [[National Trust]]. It is part of the West Lizard [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] and is in the [[Cornwall Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty]]. The Kynance Café, which opened for business in 1929, relied on spring water and on a generator for power. When the café became the property of the National Trust in 1999, the Trust renovated it and provided mains water and electricity. Access is via the [[South West Coast Path#West Cornwall|coastal footpath]] from the nearby National Trust car park.<ref name="NT F&A">{{cite web|title=Lizard Point and Knynance Cove: Facilities and access|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/lizard-point-and-kynance-cove/facilities-and-access/|website=nationaltrust.org.uk/|publisher=National Trust|accessdate=3 July 2014}}</ref>

==Geography and geology==
Much of the Lizard peninsula is known for its botany and geology, and about 375 million years ago the molten rock, which eventually became the Lizard, was about 10 km below the surface of the Earth and under immense heat and pressure. One of the rocks ([[peridotite]]) is rich in [[magnesium]] and [[iron]], and changed through heat and pressure to [[serpentinite]] as it pushed upwards from the [[Mohorovičić discontinuity|Moho]], the boundary of the Earth's [[Crust (geology)|crust]] and [[Mantle (geology)|mantle]]. It finally reached the crust's surface, about 30° south of the equator as part of an [[Mid-ocean ridge|ocean ridge]], in the [[Rheic Ocean]]. Over the next 80 million years the Rheic Ocean disappeared and the mass of rock headed north crossing the equator about 250 million years ago. The rock mass, which became the Lizard peninsula, passed the [[Tropic of Cancer]] less than 100 million years ago and finally reached 50° north at about the start of the last [[Quaternary glaciation|Ice Age]].<ref name=bates>{{cite book|last1=Bates|first1=Robin|last2=Scolding|first2=Bill|title=Beneath the Skin of The Lizard|date=2000|publisher=Cornwall County Council|location=Truro|isbn=1-898166-09-9}}</ref> 

There are two types of serpentine at Kynance: bastite and [[tremolite]]. The rocks at the car park, cliffs to the south and the path to the cove are bastite serpentine, which is the primary serpentine on the Lizard. The rock is coarse-grained with large shiny crystals of bastite which give a flecked appearance. The islands and stacks within the cove and the valley are of tremolite serpentine which is fine-grained and banded. Tremolite is different from bastite serpentine because it was subject to higher pressure within the crust.<ref name=bates/> Kynance Cove is an important site for geologists because of the exposures of the two types of [[Ophiolite|ophiolitic]] serpentinite, together with granite and gneiss pods within the serpentine. The area has been designated as a [[Geological Conservation Review]] site.<ref name=sssi>{{cite web|title=West Lizard|url=http://www.sssi.naturalengland.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1000670.pdf|website=Natural England|accessdate=30 November 2014|archive-date=24 October 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121024232946/http://www.sssi.naturalengland.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1000670.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Kynance Cove (Igneous Rocks of South-west England)|url=http://jncc.defra.gov.uk/default.aspx?page=4174&gcr=1017|website=JNCC|accessdate=30 November 2014}}</ref>
[[File:Kynance Cove, The Lizard, Cornwall, England 12Sept2017 arp.jpg|thumb|left|The [[National Trust]] cafe at Kynance Cove]]
There are a number of small tidal islands and [[Stack (geology)|stacks]] within Kynance Cove which were formed because the tremolite serpentine was broken into blocks and invaded by other types of rock, including [[granite]] and [[basalt]]. These softer rocks were eroded by the sea and the four largest stacks from left to right are The Bishop, Gull Rock, [[Asparagus Island]] and Steeple Rock.<ref name=bates/><ref name="Cornwall Beaches">{{cite web|title=Kynance Cove|url=http://cornwallbeaches.org.uk/South-Coast-West-Cornwall/Kynance-Cove.pdf|website=cornwallbeaches.org.uk|publisher=Cornwall's Beaches|accessdate=3 July 2014}}</ref> It was thought that Asparagus Island, which is cut off on almost every high tide, was connected to the mainland by a sand [[tombolo]].<ref name="Helston History Matthews">{{cite web|last1=Matthews|first1=Graham G.|title=Kynance Cove|url=http://www.helstonhistory.co.uk/around-the-lizard/kynance-cove/|website=www.helstonhistory.co.uk|publisher=Helston History|accessdate=3 July 2014}}</ref> The winter storms washed the sand away to reveal a rocky ridge, probably formed more than 100,000 years ago when sea levels were higher.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Reavealed by the storms |journal=Wild Cornwall |date=Summer 2014 |issue=124 |pages=10–11 |url=http://www.cornwallwildlifetrust.org.uk/Resources/Cornwall%20Wildlife%20Trust/PDF%20Documents/Wild_Cornwall_and_Wild_Scilly_magazine_summer_2014_issue_124.pdf |accessdate=31 March 2015 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20150918222631/http://www.cornwallwildlifetrust.org.uk/Resources/Cornwall%20Wildlife%20Trust/PDF%20Documents/Wild_Cornwall_and_Wild_Scilly_magazine_summer_2014_issue_124.pdf |archivedate=18 September 2015 }}</ref> 

At about half-tide a snorting can be heard – the sound of the ''Devil's bellows'' a [[Blowhole (geology)|blowhole]] on Asparagus Island which was caused by the sea tunnelling along a fault.<ref name=bates/> A second blowhole, the Post Office is so named because there is enough suction to post a letter in it.<ref name=lawman>{{cite book|last1=Lawman|first1=Jean|title=A Natural History of the Lizard Peninsula|date=1994|publisher=Institute of Cornish Studies and Dyllansow Truran|location=Redruth and Truro|isbn=1-85022-071-9}}</ref>

==Wildlife==
[[File:Kynance Cove hello.jpg|alt=Colourful Kynance Cove Cliff|thumb|A view from one of Kynance Cove's many hills]]
Kynance Cove was the venue for the first British record of [[Athetis hospes|Porter's rustic]] (''Athetis hospes''), a rare migrant moth from southern Europe.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hicks|first1=Michael E|title=Moths on Scilly|journal=Isles of Scilly Bird and Natural History Review 2000|date=2001|issue=1|pages=176–7}}</ref>

==Popular culture==
Kynance Cove features in the [[And Then There Were None (TV series)|2015 production]] of [[Agatha Christie]]’s ''[[And Then There Were None]]'', a [[historical drama|period drama]] of three daily episodes first broadcast on 26 December 2015.<ref>{{cite web|title=Hollywood stars come to Kynance|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/features/hollywood-stars-come-to-kynance|website=National Trust|accessdate=21 December 2015}}</ref>
It is also used as a location for the TV series [[Poldark (2015 TV series)|''Poldark'']], as Ross Poldark’s beloved Nampara, and in the episode ''The Devil's Foot'' from ''[[Sherlock Holmes (1984 TV series)|The Return of Sherlock Holmes]]''. Kynance Cove was used in seasons 1 and 2 of the [[HBO]] series [[House of the Dragon|''House of the Dragon'']] as a Velaryon camp.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hibbs |first=James |date=20 January 2021 |title=Where was House of the Dragon filmed? |url=https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/fantasy/house-dragon-filming-locations-sets/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221008024851/https://www.radiotimes.com/tv/fantasy/house-dragon-filming-locations-sets/ |archive-date=8 October 2022 |access-date=2 November 2025 |website=Radio Times}}</ref>  Recently, filming for the [[Harry Potter (TV series)|''Harry Potter'' TV series]] has taken place at the cove.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Parkman |first=Chloe |date=13 October 2025 |title=Filming of Harry Potter is 'massive' for Devon and Cornwall |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdrzl3v3m14o |access-date=2 November 2025 |website=BBC News |language=en-GB}}</ref> In film it has been used for additional shots for the planet [[Ahch-To]] in [[Star Wars: The Last Jedi|''Star Wars: The Last Jedi'']],<ref>{{Cite web |date=4 May 2025 |title=May the Fourth Be With You: Star Wars Filming Locations You Can Visit in the UK |url=https://entertainment-now.com/2025/05/may-the-fourth-be-with-you-star-wars-filming-locations-you-can-visit-in-the-uk/ |access-date=2 November 2025 |website=Entertainment Now |language=en-GB}}</ref> and featured in [[The Thief of Bagdad (1940 film)|''The Thief of Bagdad'']].<ref>{{Cite web |title=PnP FAQ - Section 2.5. Where were the films made? |url=https://powell-pressburger.org/FAQ/FAQ25.html#:~:text=Studio:%20Shepperton%20Studios,(Philip%20Armstrong%20Scott%20segment) |access-date=2 November 2025 |website=powell-pressburger.org}}</ref>

The '''Godolphin Estate''' is a [[National Trust]] property situated in [[Godolphin Cross]], {{convert|7|km|mi|abbr=on}} north-west of [[Helston]] in [[Cornwall]], England. The house is a Grade I [[listed building]].

==History==
The estate was the seat of the [[Duke of Leeds|Dukes of Leeds]] and the [[Earl of Godolphin|Earls of Godolphin]]. It contains a [[Tudor period|Tudor]]/[[Stuart period|Stuart]] mansion, complete with early formal gardens, dating from c. 1500, and [[Elizabethan era|Elizabethan]] stables of around 1600. The present house is the remnant of a larger mansion. From 1786 it was owned by the Dukes of Leeds who never lived there. In 1920 [[George Osborne, 10th Duke of Leeds]] sold it to the sitting tenant Peter Quintrell Treloar. After Treloar died in 1922, the following year his wife sold it to James Penna, an agricultural engineer. Penna died in 1926 and his son James Henry lived there until his death in 1935. In that year it was bought C.B. Stevens, a local man, who sold the house and estate to artist [[Walter Elmer Schofield]] in 1937.<ref>David Tovey, ''Creating A Splash - The St. Ives Society of Artists - The First 25 Years (1927-1952)'' (Hilmarton Manor Press, 2003).</ref> Schofield's architect son Sydney restored the mansion, and received it as a wedding present from his parents. In 2000, his widow, Mary Schofield, sold the wider estate to the [[National Trust]], and in 2007 the Trust bought the house, gardens and farm-yard. The Trust carried out a major conservation project of the architecture of the North Range (the historic front) to prevent it from further decay and collapse. The house is open to the public on certain days. The estate measures {{convert|550|acre|ha}} and includes Godolphin Hill which provides views over west Cornwall. More than four hundred recorded archaeological features range from [[Bronze Age Britain|Bronze Age]] enclosures to 19th-century [[mining|mine]] buildings. The Trust has been improving public access to the Estate.<ref name=telegraph2007-08-09 />

The large village of [[Godolphin Cross]] (sometimes Crossroads), in the parish of [[Breage, Cornwall|Breage]], adjoins the estate to the east. Amenities include a primary school.

==House and gardens==
Godolphin House is located at {{gbmapping|SW 601 318}}. Various events are held throughout the year.<ref name=NTevents /> The house is approached from the north and consists of three wings around a square courtyard and the front wall of a further building on the south side. The main buildings originally stood to the south of this with two projecting wings. One room of the 16th-century remains in the east range; this has [[linenfold]] panelling. Opposite the hall range is the [[Jacobean architecture|Jacobean]] range; the north side is castellated and has a [[loggia]] of seven bays on the ground floor. Stylistic features here appear to be of the mid 17th-century and suggest that the accepted date for the house of after 1712 is very unlikely.<ref name=Pevsner /><ref name=Listed /> The house is available as a [[Vacation rental|holiday let]] for approximately three weeks each month when it is not open to the public.<ref name=nationaltrustcottages /><ref name=guardian2011-10-28 />

===Historic listing designations===
Godolphin House is a [[listed building]], recorded at the highest designation, Grade I.<ref>{{NHLE|num=1158437|desc=Godolphin House|grade=I|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref> Three other structures on the estate, the stables,<ref>{{NHLE|num=1158586|desc=Stabling and cobbled pavements adjoining Godolphin House|grade=I|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref> the [[Courtyard|forecourt]] walls,<ref>{{NHLE|num=1142259|desc=Forecourt walls, stiles and mounting block at Godolphin House|grade=I|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref> and a [[blowing house]] used for the [[smelting]] of [[tin]] are also listed at Grade I.<ref>{{NHLE|num=1142264|desc=Blowing House and attached walls north-east of Blowing House Cottage on the Godolphin Estate|grade=I|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref> A number of buildings on the wider estate have Grade II listings: two sets of gates and [[gatepier]]s on the drive to the house,<ref>{{NHLE|num=1142263|desc=Gate Piers and Flanking Walls at Approximately 600 Metres North of Godolphin House|grade=II|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref><ref>{{NHLE|num=1311297|desc=Gate Piers and Gates at Approximately 200 Metres North of Godolphin House|grade=II|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref>
and some garden walls;<ref>{{NHLE|num=1328323|desc=King's Garden Walls, Rear Yard (South) Walls and Attached Buildings|grade=II|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref> three buildings related to the tin works, a [[counting house]],<ref>{{NHLE|num=1142224|desc=Godolphin Count House|grade=II|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref> a cottage attached to the Blowing House,<ref>{{NHLE|num=1158971|desc=Blowing House Cottage|grade=II|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref> and a pound which may have been used for the storage of [[gunpowder]];<ref>{{NHLE|num=1328325|desc=Pound at Approximately 200 Metres West of Godolphin House|grade=II|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref> and a range of ancillary agricultural buildings; a [[cider house]],<ref>{{NHLE|num=1158908|desc=Cider House at Approximately 100 Metres North East of Godolphin House|grade=II|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref> a [[piscina]] and parts of a [[Fruit press|cider press]],<ref>{{NHLE|num=1142260|desc=Piscina and Apple Crusher at Approximately 11 Metres North of Godolphin House|grade=II|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref> a [[Intensive pig farming|piggery]],<ref>{{NHLE|num=1158777|desc=Piggery at Approximately 100 Metres West of Godolphin House|grade=II|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref> a barn,<ref>{{NHLE|num=1142261|desc=Barn and Mangel House at Approximately 100 Metres South West of Godolphin House|grade=II|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref> a [[granary]],<ref>{{NHLE|num=1311355|desc=Granary at Approximately 80 Metres South West of Godolphin House|grade=II|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref> a cart shed,<ref>{{NHLE|num=1328324|desc=Cartshed at Approximately 80 Metres South West of Godolphin House|grade=II|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref> and two sets of farm buildings.<ref>{{NHLE|num=1158786|desc=Farm Buildings on West Side of Cow Yard, Including Cobbled Pavements at Approximately 200 Metres South of Godolphin House|grade=II|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref><ref>{{NHLE|num=1142262|desc=Farm Buildings and Wall on East Side of Cow Yard Approximately 200 Metres South of Godolphin House|grade=II|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref>

The Godolphin Estate is part of the [[Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape]], a [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/cornwall/godolphin/history-of-godolphin|title=History of Godolphin|publisher=[[National Trust]]|access-date=10 November 2024}}</ref>

===Local lore===
[[Image:Sidney Godolphin, 1st Earl of Godolphin by Sir Godfrey Kneller, Bt.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Sidney Godolphin, 1st Earl of Godolphin]] by Sir [[Godfrey Kneller]]]]
A custom first recorded in the 18th century, but which may date to the 14th, was enacted yearly on [[Presentation of Jesus at the Temple|Candlemas day]] (2 February) until 1921. Godolphin and St Aubyn{{Clarify|date=January 2025}} wagered their respective seats on a race between two snails; Godolphin, losing, pricked his snail which curled up and lost the race. St Aubyn instead of claiming Godolphin's estate imposed an annual custom. The [[Reeve (England)|reeve]] of Lambourne knocked on the door of the great hall of Godolphin Court and demanded to be let in. He would jump on the table and demand 'rents duties and customs'. These were paid in a large quart of strong beer, a loaf of wheaten bread and cheese of similar value and 2s 8d.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Anon|title=Don't bet on snails|journal=Mollusc World|date=2006|issue=11|page=7}}</ref>

'''Lawrence House''' is a [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] [[townhouse]] in [[Launceston, Cornwall|Launceston]], [[Cornwall]]. Built in 1753, the house is a [[National Trust]] property and a [[Grade II* listed]] building. It is leased to Launceston Town Council and used as a local museum.

==The house==
Lawrence House is a [[Grade II* listed]] building being No 9 and 9a, Castle Street, Launceston, the house, the museum and the forecourt wall all being covered by the listing. The property was first listed on 27 February 1950 under the designation "Castle Street No.9 Lawrence House, The Mayor's Parlour and Borough Museum".<ref name="NHLE"/> [[John Betjeman]] described the street as "having the most perfect collection of 18th Century townhouses in Cornwall".<ref name=Museumabout>{{cite web |url=http://lawrencehousemuseum.org.uk/about/ |title=About Lawrence House |work=Lawrence House Museum |publisher=Visit Cornwall |accessdate=11 August 2016}}</ref>

The property is a red brick town house laid to [[Flemish bond]], with two storeys as well as a basement and an attic. The roof is slated and steep with red brick chimneys and the gable end of the cross wing is on the right. An inscription reads "1753" and "HL" and another on the right wing reads "1913". The upper storey has five windows, the right hand one being a [[Venetian window]] with moulded hood. The doorway is central and has a [[pediment]]ed porch with [[pilaster]]s and consoles, and the four-panel door has a fan window above. There are two original pedimented roof [[dormer]]s, each with a 6-pane sash window. The interior has many original features including a grained basement staircase, panelling, plasterwork, moulded ceiling cornices and chimney-pieces.<ref name="NHLE">{{National Heritage List for England| num=1206174  |desc=Lawrence House and Museum and forecourt wall |grade=II* |accessdate=18 October 2015}}</ref>

Lawrence House is owned by the [[National Trust]] and leased to Launceston Town Council, who use it as a local museum and civic centre. The museum houses a collection of costumes from Victorian and more recent times on the first floor, and numerous exhibits and much information about the local history of the area on the ground floor.<ref name=Museumexhibits>{{cite web |url=http://lawrencehousemuseum.org.uk/exhibits/ |title=Exhibits |work=Lawrence House Museum |publisher=Visit Cornwall |accessdate=11 August 2016}}</ref>  During the summer season, some of the exhibits are changed around at intervals to freshen the display. 
The museum is currently{{when|date=January 2025}} closed for repair. Admission is free.<ref name=Museumabout/>

'''Levant Mine and Beam Engine''' is a [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] property at [[Trewellard]], [[Pendeen]], near [[St Just in Penwith|St Just]], [[Cornwall]], England, UK. Its main attraction is that it has the world's oldest [[Cornish engine|Cornish steam winding engine]] still working in its original location (and the last such engine still in steam in Cornwall).<ref name="NTHistory">{{cite web |title=History of Levant Mine and Beam Engine |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/cornwall/levant-mine-and-beam-engine/history-of-levant-mine-and-beam-engine |website=National Trust |access-date=28 April 2025}}</ref> There is also a visitor centre, a short underground tour, and the  [[South West Coast Path]] leads to [[Botallack Mine]], via a cliff-top footpath.<ref>{{cite web
|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/cornwall/levant-mine-and-beam-engine|title=Levant Mine and Beam Engine|publisher=National Trust|accessdate=2011-10-15}} (dead link 2 September 2019)</ref> 

In 1919 the engine used to transport men between the different levels of the mine failed, leading to the deaths of thirty-one men. Since 2006, the area has been part of the [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]], [[Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape]].

==Location==
[[File:Levant Mine 1.jpg|thumb|Levant Mine and ruins in 2020]]
[[File:Levant Mine 2.jpg|thumb|Looking up at Levant Mine]]
[[File:Levant Mine 3.jpg|thumb|Levant Mine Landscape. See sketch map above to locate features.]]
[[File:Levant Mine 4.jpg|thumb|Levant Mine, Cornwall in 2020]]
[[File:Lelant Engine.jpg|thumb|Levant mine: Beam winding engine, pump engine house and headgear. See map. ]]
The property is on the site of the former Levant Mine, established in 1820 and closed in 1930, where tin and copper ores were raised. The mine reached a depth of about 600 metres. It got the nickname "mine under the sea", because tunnels were driven up to 2.5 km from the cliffs under the sea. The surviving beam engine was built {{Circa|1840}} by [[Harvey's of Hayle]].<ref name="CM">{{cite web|url=http://www.museumsincornwall.org.uk/Levant-Mine-and-Beam-Engine/Cornwall-Museums/|title=Levant Mine and Beam Engine|publisher=Cornwall Museums|accessdate=24 May 2016}}</ref>

[[File:Levant-Mine Gebaeude en.jpg|thumb|center|300px|Overview sketch of the buildings and ruins of the Levant Mine (buildings and ruins still existing shown in red)]]

==History==
The mine yields both copper and tin and was opened in 1820 with twenty shares of £20 each. From first opening, to circa 1883, the mine gave a profit of £171,000 from approximately £1,300,000 worth of ore. In 1882 the mine was taken over by new owners on a 21 year lease, who replaced machinery and improved the surface-works.<ref name=cman283p7>{{cite news |last1=Croft |first1=E W (Ouit) |title=The Industries Of Penzance And Its Neighbourhood. No XX. The Mining Of St Just. 3 – Levant Mine |work=The Cornishman |issue=283 |date=13 December 1883 |page=7}}</ref> 

In 1883 three shafts were open. One shaft is occupied by the man-engine, a second by a pumping-engine and the third for hauling out the skips. Since the introductions of skips, for bringing ore to the surface, two shafts were abandoned. There were six engines on site,
# pumping-engine, {{convert|45|inch}} cylinder – pumps water from the mine
# stamping, {{convert|30|inch}} cylinder – breaks up the ore
# winding-engine or whim, {{convert|26|inch}} cylinder – raises the ore to the surface
# man-engine, {{convert|24|inch}} cylinder
# crushing-machine, {{convert|18|inch}} cylinder 
# winding-engine, {{convert|14|inch}} cylinder.<ref name="ouit284">{{cite news |last1=Croft |first1=E W (Ouit) |title=The Industries of Penzance and its Neighbourhood. No XX. The Mining Of St Just. 3 – Levant Mine (continued) |work=The Cornishman |issue=284 |date=20 December 1883 |page=4}}</ref>

A description of the working conditions of the mine was described in ''[[The Cornishman (newspaper)|The Cornishman]]'' newspaper in 1883. Around 366 men, boys, and girls were employed compared with about 600 prior to 1882. The mine was worked in three, eight-hour shifts, (except on Sunday) with fifty to sixty men working underground in each shift. Access to the underground levels (i.e. passages) was by ladder and the temperature was around {{convert|92|F}}. The men were all more or less working in a nude state and sweating profusely. They were provided with spring water which was stored in huge canteens. Few are able to work underground after the age of 35.<ref name=cman283p7/><ref name="cman281p7">{{cite news |last1=Perambulating Contributor |title=Roundabout Papers No 9. A Visit To Levant Mine |work=The Cornishman |issue=281 |date=29 October 1881 |page=7}}</ref> The width of the levels are {{convert|7|feet}} high and {{convert|3-4|feet}} wide, while the width of the lode is from {{convert|6|inch}} to {{convert|3|feet}} wide. Thus a quantity of hard rock on each side of the lode has to be cut away at great expense. The levels are expanded by explosives. First a hole is made by hand-drill {{convert|20|inch}} deep, taking about two hours and the hole is charged with gunpowder. Premature ignition causes many injuries and fatalities. A {{convert|14|inch}} cylinder engine raised the ore to the surface in skips on two parallel inclines, one ascending as the other was lowered.<ref name="cman281p7"/>

=== 1919 disaster ===

On 20 October 1919 an accident killed 31 miners, when a metal bracket at the top of a rod broke on the [[man engine]]. To use the man engine, the miners stepped on to a ladder, were transported {{convert|12|feet}} up or down, climbed off onto a sollar, waited for the ladder to reset its position, then stepped back on to the ladder, repeating the process. The rod broke in several pieces and heavy timbers crashed down the shaft. A large scale rescue operation was able to save some of the miners. The engine was not replaced and the lower levels of the mine were abandoned.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wisdom |first1=Phil |title=Levant centenary will be marked on Sunday |work=The Cornishman |date=17 October 2019 |page=3}}</ref>

4195901.title: St Anthony Head
4195901.extract:
St Anthony Head is a National Trust property situated at the southernmost tip of the Roseland Peninsula, Cornwall, England, United Kingdom, overlooking the  entrance to one of the world's largest natural harbours: Carrick Roads and the estuary of River Fal. It preserves the former St Anthony Battery, built in 1895–97 to defend the estuary of the River Fal.
The headland is designated as part of Carricknath Point to Porthbean Beach and Lower Fal & Helford Intertidal Sites of Special Scientific Interest. At its tip lies St Anthony's Lighthouse.

'''Penrose''' ({{langx|kw|Pennros}}) is a house (in private ownership) and [[National Trust]] estate amounting to 1536 acres, east of [[Porthleven]] and in the civil parish of [[Sithney]], [[Cornwall]], England.<ref name=OS203>{{cite map|title=Ordnance Survey: Landranger map sheet 203 ''Land's End & Isles of Scilly (St Ives & Lizard Point)''|ISBN=978-0-319-23289-7|publisher=Ordnance Survey|date=2009}}</ref><ref>Ordnance Survey get-a-map SW6403325820</ref> The estate includes [[Loe Pool]] and Loe Bar which was given into the ownership of the National Trust in 1974 by [[Lieutenant commander (Royal Navy)|Lt. Cdr.]] J. P. Rogers, and stretches along the coast to [[Gunwalloe]].<ref name=nt>Le Messurier, B. and Luck, L. (1998) "Loe Pool and Mount's Bay. No. 12 in The National Trust Coast of Cornwall series of leaflets".</ref> The estate was owned by the Penrose family for several hundred years before 1771 when it was bought for £11,000 by the Rogers family,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.lovelycornwall.org.uk/|title=Lovely Cornwall|website=www.lovelycornwall.org.uk|language=en|access-date=2018-10-21}}</ref> whose descendants still reside in Penrose House.

==Toponymy==
'"Penrose'" means 'head of the moor' (or according to [[Craig Weatherhill]] 'end/head of a hill-spur') in [[Cornish language|Cornish]]. This Penrose was formerly Penrose Methleigh (Penros Methle, 1367) i.e. 'end/head of a hill-spur at [[Methleigh]]'.<ref name="Weatherhill, Craig 2009 p. 54">[[Weatherhill, Craig]] (2009). ''A Concise Dictionary of Cornish Place-Names''. Westport, Co. Mayo: Evertype. {{ISBN|9781904808220}}; p. 54</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Robert Williams|title=Lexicon Cornu-britannicum: A Dictionary of the Ancient Celtic Language of Cornwall|url=https://archive.org/details/lexiconcornubri00willgoog|year=1865|publisher=Roderic}}</ref> The first documentation of an owner here – John de Penrose – was in 1281.<ref name=nt/>

There are seven other places named Penrose in Cornwall, in the parishes of [[Breage]], [[Budock]], [[Luxulyan]], [[Sennen]], [[St Breward]] (Penrose Burden), St Columb and [[St Ervan]].<ref name="Weatherhill, Craig 2009 p. 54"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://penroseburden.com/|title=Penrose Burden - Bodmin, Cornwall|publisher=Penroseburden.com|accessdate=7 January 2015}}</ref>

==House and estate==
===Penrose House===
Penrose House is located at OS Grid Ref: [https://tools.wmflabs.org/geohack/geohack.php?params=50.0852_N_-5.29866_E_globe:earth&language=en SW 640 258]. The current [[Grade II listed]] house consists of an irregular square plan ranged around a small courtyard with 17th-century U-shaped plan front to the northwest. The 17th-century country house was constructed for the Penrose family, probably for John Penrose who died in 1679; remodelled and extended from c. 1788 for John Rogers and c. 1832 for the Reverend John Rogers; extended 1863 by William Webb for John Jope Rogers; remodelled 1867; buttery added 1868 and centre of the elevation towards Loe Pool rebuilt 1927–28.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/101196347-penrose-manor-house-porthleven#.W9CybvZFzIU|title=Penrose Manor House, Porthleven, Cornwall|website=britishlistedbuildings.co.uk|access-date=2018-10-24}}</ref><ref>Beacham, Peter & Pevsner, Nikolaus (2014). ''Cornwall''. New Haven: Yale University Press. {{ISBN|978-0-300-12668-6}}; p. 410</ref>
[[File:PenroseBathHouse.jpg|alt=Bath house and well head|thumb|The bath house and well head east of Penrose Manor]]

===Bath house and well head east of Penrose Manor House===
Bath house and well head east of Penrose Manor House are located at OS Grid Ref: [https://tools.wmflabs.org/geohack/geohack.php?params=50.086433_N_-5.29813_E_globe:earth&language=en SW 641 259]. The Tudor Gothic style Bath house was built in 1840 for John Rogers. The bath house contains a slate lined bath on the right and a rounded well head to the rear.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/101196348-bath-house-and-well-head-east-of-penrose-manor-house-porthleven#.W9CycPZFzIU|title=Bath House and Well Head East of Penrose Manor House, Porthleven, Cornwall|author=Good Stuff|website=britishlistedbuildings.co.uk|access-date=2018-10-24}}</ref>

===Carpenter's shop===
The carpenter's shop, situated 100 metres to the southwest of Penrose Manor House at  OS Grid Ref: SW 640 256, was built pre-1833 for John Rogers.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/101196349-carpenters-shop-100-metres-south-west-of-penrose-manor-house-porthleven#.W9C79vZFzIV|title=Carpenter's Shop 100 Metres South West of Penrose Manor House, Porthleven, Cornwall|author=Good Stuff|website=britishlistedbuildings.co.uk|access-date=2018-10-24}}</ref>

===The Loe===
[[The Loe]], also known as Loe Pool and historically called La Loo, is the largest natural freshwater lake (50 hectares (120 acres)) in [[Cornwall]] and now in the ownership of the [[National Trust]]. Lieutenant commander Rogers's gift to the National Trust was made in 1974; a condition of the gift was that the Loe should be kept as a place of great beauty for people to enjoy without distraction. Boating, swimming and fishing are not allowed.

==History==
Penrose (or at least some land) was held by the Penrose family pre-1269. The estate grew as a result of various grants of land and inheritances some of which resulted from marriages linking the Penroses with other leading Cornish families including: St Aubyn, Tremayne, Methele, Erissey, Killigrew and Rashleigh. Between 1750 and 1770 Penrose was bought by Hugh Rogers. Hugh Rogers and his son the Reverend John Rogers carried out many of the major alterations and additions at Penrose.<ref name=":0" />

===Descent of Penrose estate===

====John de Penrose====
John de Penrose was the owner in 1281.<ref name=nt/>

====John Rogers of Treassowe====
John Rogers of Treassowe, [[Ludgvan]], died in the late 17th-century, leaving a son (John) by his wife Florence. The coat of arms of [[Rogers (surname)|Rogers]] of Penrose and Treassowe is Arg. a chevron between three bucks trippant Sa.; their crest is a buck as in the arms.<ref>Pascoe, W. H. (1979) ''A Cornish Armory''. Padstow: Lodenek Press; p. 92</ref>

====John Rogers (1636–1725)====
John Rogers married Thomasine, daughter of Hugh Bawden of Guddern, [[Kea, Cornwall|Kea]], leaving a son John.<ref name="burke">{{cite book|last1=Burke|first1=John|title=A Genealogical and Heraldic History of the Commoners of Great Britain and Ireland, Volume 1|date=1835|publisher=Henry Colburn|location=London|page=[https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_QisAAAAAQAAJ/page/n315 299]|url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_QisAAAAAQAAJ|accessdate=19 November 2016}}</ref>

====John Rogers (1690–1768)====
John Rogers married his cousin Aurelia, daughter of Hugh Bawden of Guddern, leaving a son Hugh.<ref name="burke"/>

====Hugh Rogers (1732–)====
Hugh Rogers married Anne, daughter of James Bishop of St Columb, leaving a son John. He purchased the estate in 1771 from Mrs. Cummings, the heir to the Penrose Estate.<ref name=cman95>{{cite news|title=Funeral Of Mr John Jope Rogers Of Penrose|work=The Cornishman|issue=95|date=6 May 1880|page=4}}</ref>
<ref name="burke"/>

====John Rogers (1750–1832)====
[[John Rogers (1750–1832)|John Rogers]] (15 August 1750 – 22 February 1832) was married to Margaret, the daughter of Francis Basset of Tehidy;<ref name="Stuff">{{Cite web|url=https://britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/101196347-penrose-manor-house-porthleven#.W8yfvfZFzIU|title=Penrose Manor House, Porthleven, Cornwall|author=Good Stuff|website=britishlistedbuildings.co.uk|access-date=2018-10-21}}</ref> he was [[Member of Parliament (UK)|MP]] for [[Helston (UK Parliament constituency)|Helston]], Cornwall, from 1784 to 1786.<ref name="burke"/>

====John Rogers (1778–1856)====
The Rev. [[John Rogers (divine)|John Rogers]] (17 July 1778 – 12 June 1856) succeeded to the Penrose and [[Helston]] estates of about ten thousand acres (40 km²), comprising the manors of Penrose, Helston, Carminow, Winnianton, and various other estates in Cornwall, including several mines, in February 1832 on the death of his father. According to the obituary, of his son John Jope Rogers (published in [[The Cornishman (newspaper)|The Cornishman]]) the Penrose lands had been acquired in 1771 by his grandfather, Hugh Rogers, and the Helston lands in 1798 by his father. Rogers died at Penrose on 12 June 1856, and was the first occupant of the family vault at [[Sithney]] churchyard.<ref name=cman95/> He was an Anglican priest, mine-owner, botanist, mineralogist, and scholar of Hebrew and [[Syriac language|Syriac]].

====John Jope Rogers (1816–1880)====
[[John Jope Rogers]] (16 February 1816 – 24 April 1880) was an author and [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] MP for Helston from 1859 to 1865.

====John Peverell Rogers (1846–1928)====
John Peverell (born 7 November 1846 – 21 August 1928) was a captain in the [[Royal Regiment of Artillery]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=von Arx|first1=Rolf|title=Reverend Rogers' Quest For Mining Riches|journal=British Mining Memoirs|date=1997|issue=59|pages=97–107|publisher=Northern Mine Research Society}}</ref>

====John Lionel Rogers (1880–1961)====
Captain John Lionel Rogers, who died on 5 November 1961, was married to Caroline Ford of Pengreep,<ref name="Stuff"/> without issue; his younger brother gave up his right of succession in favour of his eldest son, Lieutenant Commander J. P, Rogers.

====John Peverell Rogers (1925–2012)====
Lt. Cdr. John Peverell Rogers (1925 – 7 July 2012) was married to Angela, having two sons Nigel (deceased) and Charles (deceased 2018). He served in the Royal Navy until 1962 and ran the estate for around ten years, having taken it over from his uncle Lionel Rogers. In 1974 he handed a large part of the estate, including farms, properties and woodland, to the National Trust and continued to run the remainder himself.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.falmouthpacket.co.uk/news/9822576.tributes-paid-after-death-of-penrose-estate-owner/|title=Tributes paid after death of Penrose Estate owner|website=Falmouth Packet|language=en|access-date=2018-10-21}}</ref>

====Charles Rogers (1956-2018)====
Charles Rogers died in August 2018, apparently without an heir.<ref>Daily Telegraph, 25 May 2019</ref>

====Jordan Adlard Rogers (1987–)====
In 2019, Jordan Adlard Rogers proved he was the son of the previous owner, by a DNA test, and inherited the remaining parts of the estate still owned by the Roger’s family and the right to reside in Penrose House. <ref>Steve Bird [https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2019/05/25/grandmother-new-lord-manor-shuns-50-million-mansion-family-home/ Grandmother of new lord of the manor shuns £50 million mansion for family home on Cornish estate]; The Daily Telegraph; 25 May 2019</ref>
